tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

# Self-Authored Direction

> If direction isn't provided from above, you have to produce it yourself. The cost of waiting is constant fire-fighting; the cost of authoring it is the work of choosing.

## Why it matters

In a role where leadership doesn't hand down explicit weekly objectives, the absence of structure is mistaken for freedom. It isn't. It's an open door for everyone else's priorities to walk in and fill the vacuum. Without self-authored direction, the day shape is dictated by the inbox: meetings to schedule, emails to reply to, sponsorships to discuss, partnerships to chase. None of that is *bad* — but none of it ladders up to a stated objective unless you do the laddering.

The discipline is: **daily intentions feed weekly priorities feed department objectives**. Break the chain at any link and you're running around like chickens with your heads cut off.

## Evidence / origin

- Friday 2026-05-22 morning briefing: 5 emails needing reply, 3 meetings to schedule, 1 form owed, 1 FYI — *all* externally initiated. None framed by a stated weekly objective.
- Self-observation during the [[2026-05-22-interview]]: "I can get led astray. Not everything is important."
- The Aranda practice-planning meeting [[2026-05-22_PreSummer_Planning]] is the *same dynamic at the team level* — the head coach is now imposing a deliberate practice framework (green/yellow/red days) so the season isn't driven by whatever the day happens to throw at the staff.
- 2026-06-02 [[2026-06-02-interview]]: "a lot of really talented people who need better, stronger direction so we can achieve some really cool things." The bottleneck isn't talent — it's direction, and supplying it is the unit's job.

## Connections
- [[planning-windows-compound]] — self-authored direction is hardest to build mid-season; planning windows are when you set it
- [[adoption-is-the-bottleneck]] — **update (2026-05-28):** this note solved only the *what*. The harder constraint is getting other people to follow self-authored direction; direction nobody adopts is isolation, not traction.
- [[the-daily-on-ramp]] — the daily tier of the ladder; the morning brief is how authored direction survives contact with the day.
- *Three-tier laddering* (daily → weekly → quarterly OKRs) — **now built (2026-06-02):** daily brief → weekly Thursday check-in → quarterly OKR score.
- Future note: *The cost of saying no* — every yes to a marginal project is a no to a stated objective

## Open questions

- ~~What's the right cadence for re-authoring direction? Weekly review? Monthly?~~ → **resolved (2026-06-02):** weekly Thursday unit check-in + monthly objective rebalance + end-of-quarter score (the OKR operating playbook).
- ~~How do you make self-authored objectives stick when the org doesn't reinforce them?~~ → reframed in [[adoption-is-the-bottleneck]]: it's a consensus/adoption problem, and when the velocity mismatch is large enough, exit is a legitimate answer.
- ~~Which tool/workflow makes daily → weekly → department traceability cheap enough to maintain?~~ → **resolved (2026-06-02):** an OKR tracker for the weekly tier + [[the-daily-on-ramp]] for the daily tier.

# The Daily On-Ramp

> Self-authored direction doesn't fail at the strategy layer — it fails at the daily on-ramp. The cheap fix is a standing morning brief: *what didn't get done yesterday → what must get done today → the week's big rocks.* That's the mechanism that converts authored direction into daily momentum.

## Why it matters

You can have a sharp set of objectives and still lose the day. The gap between "I know my priorities" and "I worked my priorities" is the first 15 minutes after the workstation boots. Without a deliberate on-ramp, the inbox sets the agenda and good intentions get back-filled by whatever arrives first — and things fall through the cracks not because they were forgotten in principle but because nothing re-surfaced them at the start of the day.

The brief is small on purpose. Three moves — yesterday's incompletes, today's must-dos, the week's big rocks — make the daily→weekly→quarterly ladder *visible at the moment of choosing*, which is the only moment it can change behavior. It's the daily counterpart to the weekly OKR check-in: the check-in sets the week, the brief spends it.

## Evidence / origin

- [[2026-06-02-interview]]: surprised by how little progress a Tuesday produced; named the fix as a morning brief that runs from yesterday's incompletes to today's must-dos to the week's big rocks, "so there's constant momentum and things don't fall through the cracks."
- Directly answers the open question left in [[self-authored-direction]]: *which workflow makes daily → weekly → department traceability cheap enough to maintain?*
- A partial scaffold already exists in the vault (`morning-briefings/`); the insight is to make it a disciplined daily ritual that explicitly ladders to the week's big rocks, not just a list.

## Connections
- [[self-authored-direction]] — the brief is *how* authored direction survives contact with the day; resolves its cadence/tool open questions.
- [[answers-without-questions]] — distilling many ideas into the day's few right actions is the same discipline applied at the daily scale.
- [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]] — **update (2026-06-04):** the generated-vs-hand-written question is downstream of a bigger one — *delivery*. The brief generated perfectly on 06-04 and still failed because nothing put it in front of me. Generation is moot if the surface isn't surfaced.
- The OKR operating playbook's weekly Thursday check-in is the weekly tier; this note is the daily tier beneath it.

## Open questions
- Should the brief be generated (from the OKR tracker + yesterday's log) or hand-written each morning? Generated lowers friction; hand-written forces the choosing. *(2026-06-04: hand-written's hidden advantage is delivery — you read it because you wrote it.)*
- What's the minimum that still works on a chaotic day — can it survive at 3 lines?
- **Delivery channel (open, blocking):** the cron writes to `morning-briefings/YYYY-MM-DD.md` but doesn't deliver it. Email at 07:47? Surface at first session of the day? Needs a fix — see [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]].

# Keep the main thing the main thing

> There will always be work that personally excites you but doesn't advance the larger mission. The discipline is not avoiding distraction once — it's expecting the pull constantly and re-choosing the primary thing anyway.

## Why it matters

Infrastructure days, vendor calls, and side projects all feel productive. The failure mode isn't laziness — it's enthusiasm pointed at the wrong target. A day can fly by fully "dialed in" and still not move the mission.

Don't get sidetracked by a bunch of frivolous stuff that maybe personally excites you but does not help you with the larger things you're trying to accomplish."

# Applied Performance — Unit OKRs (2026–27)

## Vision (North Star)
**Be the best applied performance department in the country.**

That's the bar. A KR is "done" only at a level a top-5 program would recognize, not just "we did a thing."

## Mission (how we get there)
Turn Baylor's athlete data into decisions that keep athletes available and performing, build the data and performance literacy of the people who use it, and produce original research that advances both the program and the university's R1 mission.

## Structure (v3)
Three permanent **service pillars** — Data Systems & Analytics, Education, Research & Development — plus one **enabling objective** (Leadership & Visibility) that the new responsibilities document made explicit: the unit now delivers through people and processes Eric directs, not only through work Eric performs. Role-language definitions (Oversee, Assist, Support-and-guide, Unified) live in [[Applied-Performance-JD-2026/CONTEXT]].

97	# Self-Authored Direction
98	
99	> If direction isn't provided from above, you have to produce it yourself. The cost of waiting is constant fire-fighting; the cost of authoring it is the work of choosing.
100	
101	## Why it matters
102	
103	In a role where leadership doesn't hand down explicit weekly objectives, the absence of structure is mistaken for freedom. It isn't. It's an open door for everyone else's priorities to walk in and fill the vacuum. Without self-authored direction, the day shape is dictated by the inbox: meetings to schedule, emails to reply to, sponsorships to discuss, partnerships to chase. None of that is *bad* — but none of it ladders up to a stated objective unless you do the laddering.
104	
105	The discipline is: **daily intentions feed weekly priorities feed department objectives**. Break the chain at any link and you're running around like chickens with your heads cut off.

140	# The Daily On-Ramp
141	
142	> Self-authored direction doesn't fail at the strategy layer — it fails at the daily on-ramp. The cheap fix is a standing morning brief: *what didn't get done yesterday → what must get done today → the week's big rocks.* That's the mechanism that converts authored direction into daily momentum.
143	
144	## Why it matters
145	
146	You can have a sharp set of objectives and still lose the day. The gap between "I know my priorities" and "I worked my priorities" is the first 15 minutes after the workstation boots. Without a deliberate on-ramp, the inbox sets the agenda and good intentions get back-filled by whatever arrives first — and things fall through the cracks not because they were forgotten in principle but because nothing re-surfaced them at the start of the day.
147	
148	The brief is small on purpose. Three moves — yesterday's incompletes, today's must-dos, the week's big rocks — make the daily→weekly→quarterly ladder *visible at the moment of choosing*, which is the only moment it can change behavior. It's the daily counterpart to the weekly OKR check-in: the check-in sets the week, the brief spends it.
149	
150	## Evidence / origin
151	
152	- [[2026-06-02-interview]]: surprised by how little progress a Tuesday produced; named the fix as a morning brief that runs from yesterday's incompletes to today's must-dos to the week's big rocks, "so there's constant momentum and things don't fall through the cracks."
153	- Directly answers the open question left in [[self-authored-direction]]: *which workflow makes daily → weekly → department traceability cheap enough to maintain?*
154	- A partial scaffold already exists in the vault (`morning-briefings/`); the insight is to make it a disciplined daily ritual that explicitly ladders to the week's big rocks, not just a list.
155

157	- [[self-authored-direction]] — the brief is *how* authored direction survives contact with the day; resolves its cadence/tool open questions.
158	- [[answers-without-questions]] — distilling many ideas into the day's few right actions is the same discipline applied at the daily scale.
159	- [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]] — **update (2026-06-04):** the generated-vs-hand-written question is downstream of a bigger one — *delivery*. The brief generated perfectly on 06-04 and still failed because nothing put it in front of me. Generation is moot if the surface isn't surfaced.

# Finish one project before you start the next one

> The problem was never only choosing the main thing. It is starting the next thing before the current one is finished. Picking priorities without a rule about finishing leaves a pile of started work and little that ships.

## Why it matters

Three earlier notes named the same pain from the choosing side: author your own direction, run a daily on-ramp, keep the main thing the main thing. Four months later the realization is the same, which says the gap is not in knowing what matters. The gap is at the moment a new project shows up while an old one is still open. A self-directed role has no one to say "not yet," so the rule has to be part of the process.

## Evidence / origin

- [[2026-09-14-interview]], essay seed, verbatim: "Finish one project before you start the next one."

# Self-Authored Direction

> If direction isn't provided from above, you have to produce it yourself. The cost of waiting is constant fire-fighting; the cost of authoring it is the work of choosing.

## Why it matters

In a role where leadership doesn't hand down explicit weekly objectives, the absence of structure is mistaken for freedom. It isn't. It's an open door for everyone else's priorities to walk in and fill the vacuum. Without self-authored direction, the day shape is dictated by the inbox: meetings to schedule, emails to reply to, sponsorships to discuss, partnerships to chase. None of that is *bad* — but none of it ladders up to a stated objective unless you do the laddering.

The discipline is: **daily intentions feed weekly priorities feed department objectives**. Break the chain at any link and you're running around like chickens with your heads cut off.

## Evidence / origin

- Friday 2026-05-22 morning briefing: 5 emails needing reply, 3 meetings to schedule, 1 form owed, 1 FYI — *all* externally initiated. None framed by a stated weekly objective.
- Self-observation during the [[2026-05-22-interview]]: "I can get led astray. Not everything is important."
- The Aranda practice-planning meeting [[2026-05-22_PreSummer_Planning]] is the *same dynamic at the team level* — the head coach is now imposing a deliberate practice framework (green/yellow/red days) so the season isn't driven by whatever the day happens to throw at the staff.
- 2026-06-02 [[2026-06-02-interview]]: "a lot of really talented people who need better, stronger direction so we can achieve some really cool things." The bottleneck isn't talent — it's direction, and supplying it is the unit's job.

## Connections
- [[planning-windows-compound]] — self-authored direction is hardest to build mid-season; planning windows are when you set it
- [[adoption-is-the-bottleneck]] — **update (2026-05-28):** this note solved only the *what*. The harder constraint is getting other people to follow self-authored direction; direction nobody adopts is isolation, not traction.
- [[the-daily-on-ramp]] — the daily tier of the ladder; the morning brief is how authored direction survives contact with the day.
- *Three-tier laddering* (daily → weekly → quarterly OKRs) — **now built (2026-06-02):** daily brief → weekly Thursday check-in → quarterly OKR score.
- Future note: *The cost of saying no* — every yes to a marginal project is a no to a stated objective

## Open questions

- ~~What's the right cadence for re-authoring direction? Weekly review? Monthly?~~ → **resolved (2026-06-02):** weekly Thursday unit check-in + monthly objective rebalance + end-of-quarter score (the OKR operating playbook).
- ~~How do you make self-authored objectives stick when the org doesn't reinforce them?~~ → reframed in [[adoption-is-the-bottleneck]]: it's a consensus/adoption problem, and when the velocity mismatch is large enough, exit is a legitimate answer.
- ~~Which tool/workflow makes daily → weekly → department traceability cheap enough to maintain?~~ → **resolved (2026-06-02):** an OKR tracker for the weekly tier + [[the-daily-on-ramp]] for the daily tier.

# The Daily On-Ramp

> Self-authored direction doesn't fail at the strategy layer — it fails at the daily on-ramp. The cheap fix is a standing morning brief: *what didn't get done yesterday → what must get done today → the week's big rocks.* That's the mechanism that converts authored direction into daily momentum.

## Why it matters

You can have a sharp set of objectives and still lose the day. The gap between "I know my priorities" and "I worked my priorities" is the first 15 minutes after the workstation boots. Without a deliberate on-ramp, the inbox sets the agenda and good intentions get back-filled by whatever arrives first — and things fall through the cracks not because they were forgotten in principle but because nothing re-surfaced them at the start of the day.

The brief is small on purpose. Three moves — yesterday's incompletes, today's must-dos, the week's big rocks — make the daily→weekly→quarterly ladder *visible at the moment of choosing*, which is the only moment it can change behavior. It's the daily counterpart to the weekly OKR check-in: the check-in sets the week, the brief spends it.

## Evidence / origin

- [[2026-06-02-interview]]: surprised by how little progress a Tuesday produced; named the fix as a morning brief that runs from yesterday's incompletes to today's must-dos to the week's big rocks, "so there's constant momentum and things don't fall through the cracks."
- Directly answers the open question left in [[self-authored-direction]]: *which workflow makes daily → weekly → department traceability cheap enough to maintain?*
- A partial scaffold already exists in the vault (`morning-briefings/`); the insight is to make it a disciplined daily ritual that explicitly ladders to the week's big rocks, not just a list.

## Connections
- [[self-authored-direction]] — the brief is *how* authored direction survives contact with the day; resolves its cadence/tool open questions.
- [[answers-without-questions]] — distilling many ideas into the day's few right actions is the same discipline applied at the daily scale.
- [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]] — **update (2026-06-04):** the generated-vs-hand-written question is downstream of a bigger one — *delivery*. The brief generated perfectly on 06-04 and still failed because nothing put it in front of me. Generation is moot if the surface isn't surfaced.
- The OKR operating playbook's weekly Thursday check-in is the weekly tier; this note is the daily tier beneath it.

## Open questions
- Should the brief be generated (from the OKR tracker + yesterday's log) or hand-written each morning? Generated lowers friction; hand-written forces the choosing. *(2026-06-04: hand-written's hidden advantage is delivery — you read it because you wrote it.)*
- What's the minimum that still works on a chaotic day — can it survive at 3 lines?
- **Delivery channel (open, blocking):** the cron writes to `morning-briefings/YYYY-MM-DD.md` but doesn't deliver it. Email at 07:47? Surface at first session of the day? Needs a fix — see [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]].

# Keep the main thing the main thing

> There will always be work that personally excites you but doesn't advance the larger mission. The discipline is not avoiding distraction once — it's expecting the pull constantly and re-choosing the primary thing anyway.

## Why it matters

Infrastructure days, vendor calls, and side projects all feel productive. The failure mode isn't laziness — it's enthusiasm pointed at the wrong target. A day can fly by fully "dialed in" and still not move the mission.

## Evidence / origin

End-of-day debrief, 2026-07-31 — a day spent on knowledge infrastructure and loose ends, stated verbatim as the one thing to tell a peer: "Keep the main thing the main thing. Don't get sidetracked by a bunch of frivolous stuff that maybe personally excites you but does not help you with the larger things you're trying to accomplish."

## Connections
- [[design-the-conditions-not-the-discipline]] — a tidy workspace is one condition that keeps the main thing in front of you
- [[waiting-for-the-ask-kills-the-idea]] — the tension: proactivity is good, but proactive frivolity is still frivolity

## Open questions
- What's the test for "frivolous but exciting" vs. "exploratory and mission-adjacent"? Infrastructure work sits right on that line.

# Applied Performance — Unit OKRs (2026–27)

## Vision (North Star)
**Be the best applied performance department in the country.**

That's the bar. A KR is "done" only at a level a top-5 program would recognize, not just "we did a thing."

## Mission (how we get there)
Turn Baylor's athlete data into decisions that keep athletes available and performing, build the data and performance literacy of the people who use it, and produce original research that advances both the program and the university's R1 mission.

## Structure (v3)
Three permanent **service pillars** — Data Systems & Analytics, Education, Research & Development — plus one **enabling objective** (Leadership & Visibility) that the new responsibilities document made explicit: the unit now delivers through people and processes Eric directs, not only through work Eric performs. Role-language definitions (Oversee, Assist, Support-and-guide, Unified) live in [[Applied-Performance-JD-2026/CONTEXT]].

**Cycle mechanics:** KRs are committed per semester (quarterly rhythm retired 2026-07-17 — decision 0007). Every KR is scored at the mid-semester checkpoint (on-track/off-track) and at cycle close (0.0–1.0, keep/retire/add). The biweekly Friday report to Chris is the standing pulse between checkpoints. Every KR must have its critical path inside the unit's control — no KR whose completion depends on an external party's timeline.

**Eric's protected hands-on lanes** (not delegated, not reviewed-only — built by his hands): HPI protocol and its dashboarding; technology vetting; white-paper analysis; one-off report and dashboard creation for sports. Delegation stops at these boundaries.

---

## Objective 1 — Data Systems & Infrastructure
> **The data layer is standardized, governed, and survives staff transition; sport-facing delivery is bespoke on top of it and routinely drives coaching decisions.**

*"Unified" means standardized underneath (metric definitions, data model, freshness), bespoke on top (per-sport dashboards and reports). A single all-programs dashboard is explicitly not the goal (decision 0008).*

# CONTEXT — JD Role Language Glossary

Ubiquitous language for the 2026 Athletics Performance Staff Responsibilities document (Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance) and the OKR docs built on it. Companion decisions: [[decisions]].

## Assist

Another named person owns the function and sets direction; Eric executes what they delegate. Ownership, priorities, and external accountability sit with the owner, not Eric.

> Example: AP Clinic — Courteney Tompkins owns the event; Eric takes his responsibilities from her lead. (Resolved 2026-07-16.)

## Oversee (Eric → AP staff)

Eric owns the standards, templates, and strategic direction; the staff member owns execution and the external relationships in their lane. Concretely: a weekly 1:1, pre-delivery review of any artifact leaving the department, and no direct involvement in day-to-day operations of the overseen lane.

> Example: AJ owns fall-camp planning and all FB-staff communications, including presenting the plan-vs-actual review to Aranda; Eric reviews artifacts before delivery and co-builds the analysis. (Resolved 2026-07-17.)

## Unified (data & dashboards)

Standardized underneath, bespoke on top. Unification lives in the data layer — common metric definitions, common data model, common freshness expectations — never in a single shared UI. Each sport's dashboards and reports are bespoke deliveries built on that shared foundation.

> Example: KR 1.1 — per-sport coach dashboards (FB via AJ, VB direct) on shared data standards; the HPI protocol and continuity plan are what standardize the underneath. (Resolved 2026-07-17.)

## Support and guide (Eric → BB AP GA)

Mentoring-weighted oversight: Eric teaches departmental procedures, policies, and data-management practice; the GA (Noah) executes with training wheels on. Distinct from Oversee — Noah is not yet accountable for a lane's outcomes; Eric is.

## Briefing Asset (department briefing)

The reusable core content that explains Applied Performance — the three service pillars + capability menu + one-sentence mission — as distinct from any single talk. A **deployment** is one delivery of the asset wrapped for a specific room (audience, ask, and depth vary; the model does not). Deployments are variants of the asset, never separate scopes.

> Example: v1 deployment = the admin/sport-admin briefing; head-coach variant and H&W-onboarding module are staged derivatives, not part of v1. (Resolved 2026-07-18.)

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
the approval gate never does.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
artifact, never the approval.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];

    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

> A brief that is generated but not delivered fails exactly like no brief at all. If the output lands somewhere you have to remember to go look, the tool recreates the very cracks it was built to close. Surfacing is part of the mechanism, not an afterthought.

## Why it matters

The daily on-ramp exists to stop priorities from falling through the cracks at the start of the day. Today it ran perfectly — the cron fired at 07:47, wrote a complete, well-prioritized brief (overdue items flagged, OKR check-in surfaced) — and still failed its one job, because nothing put it in front of me. A surfacing tool that requires the user to *go find* the surface isn't surfacing anything; it's just generating.

This generalizes past morning briefs. Any system whose value is "the right thing shows up at the right moment" has two halves — **generation** and **delivery** — and they fail independently. Teams over-invest in generation (better content, smarter prioritization) and treat delivery as a detail, when delivery is where the value is actually realized. A perfect report in a folder no one opens has a real-world value of zero. Design the moment of contact, not just the artifact.

## Evidence / origin

The gap was purely delivery — the mechanism writes to a vault file and has no email/notification/session-surface step.
- Mirrors the failure mode the source note already named: things fall through the cracks "not because they were forgotten in principle but because nothing re-surfaced them at the start of the day" ([[the-daily-on-ramp]]) — here the *re-surfacer itself* wasn't surfaced.

## Connections

- [[self-authored-direction]] — authored direction only survives the day if the daily reminder actually arrives.

## Open questions
- What's the delivery channel? Email at 07:47, surface at first Claude session of the day, or an OS/phone push — which one actually gets read?

# Applied Performance — OKR Operating Playbook

How the unit runs the [[Applied-Performance-OKRs-2026-27|OKRs]] week to week: who owns what, how we introduce the system, how we meet, how work gets assigned and progressed, and how the OKRs drive the actual work through the summer. Deliberately lightweight — a 3-person unit needs a weekly touch and a clear owner per result, not process overhead.

**The loop in one line:** *KR → a single next action → worked during the week → reviewed Thursday → confidence + next action updated in the tracker → repeats, laddering to the end-of-August score.*

## Ownership model
**Eric is DRI (directly responsible) on all 9 KRs** — single accountable owner. **AJ and Blake co-own** specific KRs: a co-owner drives the week-to-week work and reports status at the check-in. Eric stays accountable, removes blockers, and makes the calls.

| KR | Result (short) | DRI | Co-owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | Unified coach dashboard in weekly use (FB + VB) | Eric | AJ |
| 1.2 | Practice-load framework adopted for fall camp | Eric | AJ |
| 1.3 | Documented decision impact (≥8 logged) | Eric | AJ |
| 2.1 | Education engine runs (newsletter ×2/mo) | Eric | Blake |
| 2.2 | Reach across the three audiences | Eric | AJ |
| 2.3 | Recognition / pull (≥2 inbound requests) | Eric | — |
| 3.1 | Research repository launched (Jul 31) | Eric | Blake |
| 3.2 | ≥1 academic partnership formalized | Eric | Blake |
| 3.3 | First white paper scoped + drafted | Eric | Blake |

## Rollout — the first check-in (June 4)
No separate kickoff; the system gets introduced inside the first Thursday check-in. Run this once with AJ and Blake (~15 min before the normal round begins):

1. **Why we're doing this (3 min).** We author our own direction instead of running on inbox. The bar is "best applied performance department in the country" — every KR is "done" only at a level a top-5 program would recognize.
2. **The shape (3 min).** Three permanent pillars (Analytics & Planning · Education · R&D). Objectives are stable for the year; **KRs are committed one quarter at a time** and are **outcomes, not activity**. We score and reset at the end of August — it's iterative, not a 12-month list we ignore.
3. **Walk the live scoreboard (4 min).** Open `okr-tracker/SCOREBOARD.md`. Explain **confidence** (your honest P(hit the target by the gate)), the **status** colors, and the **trend** sparkline (momentum across weeks).
4. **Ownership + the rule (3 min).** Show the table above. Eric DRI on all; AJ/Blake co-own. **The rule: every KR always carries exactly one "next action."**
5. **Seed week one (2 min).** Each co-owner names the one next action for each KR they own (the tracker is already seeded with starting actions — confirm or replace).

## The weekly check-in (Thursdays, ~20–30 min)
Standing meeting through the summer build; **dial to biweekly once in-season**.

```
0–2 min   Open: glance at SCOREBOARD.md together.
2–20 min  KR round-robin, by objective (≤2 min each). Per KR the co-owner gives:
            • status color (🟢/🟡/🔴/✅)
            • what moved since last week
            • confidence now + why it changed
            • blocker (if any) → who clears it
            • the next action (by next Thursday)
20–27 min Eric: decisions needed · cross-KR connections · capture new items
            (don't derail) · rebalance if an objective's avg confidence is sliding.
27–30 min Update the tracker (okr.py check … per KR that moved) → ./backup.sh.
```

## How work gets assigned
- KRs are owned as **outcomes, not handed out as tasks**. The co-owner decides *how* to get there; Eric is accountable and unblocks.
- The **unit of assignment is the "next action"** — one per KR at a time, committed out loud at the check-in and stored in the tracker (`--next`). When one is done, the next is named.
- This preserves autonomy (co-owners self-direct) while keeping one always-visible next step per result.

## How work progresses
- **Confidence is the heartbeat.** Each Thursday, set an honest P(hit by gate). The trend sparkline shows momentum, not just today's number.
- **Escalation trigger:** a KR red two weeks running, or confidence falling two weeks running → Eric reallocates time / clears the blocker, or the target gets renegotiated at the month boundary.
- **Monthly (first check-in of the month):** a 5-minute zoom-out on each objective's **average confidence** — pour effort into the lagging pillar.
- **Quarterly gate (end of August):** score each KR 0.0–1.0, mark met/partial/missed, then keep · retire · add, and author the Q2 set.

## How the OKRs drive the week & month (summer)
This is the point of the whole system — the OKRs set the priorities, not the inbox.
- **The filter:** every block of weekly work should ladder to a KR or a pillar. If a chunk doesn't map to any pillar, question whether it's the unit's work.
- **In practice:** each person's weekly plan **leads with their KR next-actions** as the anchor priorities; reactive and service requests fill in *around* them, not over them.
- **The summer arc (the red → green march to the gate):**
  - **June** — stand up the engines: newsletter issue #1, dashboard unification, the decision-log habit, repo schema. (Today's 🔴 KRs.)
  - **July** — build & deliver: repo MVP (Jul 31), partner formalized, white-paper draft started, practice-load framework finalized for camp.
  - **August** — adopt & run: dashboard in real weekly use (FB + VB), framework live for fall camp, decision log filling → **gate**.

## Tracking — the scoreboard tool
Status lives in **`okr-tracker/`** (see its README), not in hand-maintained tables. Each Thursday, log what moved:
```bash
python okr-tracker/okr.py check <KR> <confidence 0.0–1.0> <green|yellow|red|met> "<note>" --next "<next action>" [--blocker "..."]
```
That regenerates **`okr-tracker/SCOREBOARD.md`** — status, confidence, progress bar, per-KR trend, and the current next action, grouped by objective. Confidence = P(hit target by gate).

## At the gate (end of August)
Set each KR's `score` (0.0–1.0 attainment) in `okrs.yaml`, mark met / partial / missed, then keep · retire · add and author the Q2 set.

```
2–20 min  KR round-robin, by objective (≤2 min each). Per KR the co-owner gives:
            • status color (🟢/🟡/🔴/✅)
            • what moved since last week
            • confidence now + why it changed
            • blocker (if any) → who clears it
            • the next action (by next Thursday)
20–27 min Eric: decisions needed · cross-KR connections · capture new items
            (don't derail) · rebalance if an objective's avg confidence is sliding.
27–30 min Update the tracker (okr.py check … per KR that moved) → ./backup.sh.
```

## How work gets assigned
- KRs are owned as **outcomes, not handed out as tasks**. The co-owner decides *how* to get there; Eric is accountable and unblocks.
- The **unit of assignment is the "next action"** — one per KR at a time, committed out loud at the check-in and stored in the tracker (`--next`). When one is done, the next is named.
- This preserves autonomy (co-owners self-direct) while keeping one always-visible next step per result.

## How work progresses
- **Confidence is the heartbeat.** Each Thursday, set an honest P(hit by gate). The trend sparkline shows momentum, not just today's number.
- **Escalation trigger:** a KR red two weeks running, or confidence falling two weeks running → Eric reallocates time / clears the blocker, or the target gets renegotiated at the month boundary.
- **Monthly (first check-in of the month):** a 5-minute zoom-out on each objective's **average confidence** — pour effort into the lagging pillar.
- **Quarterly gate (end of August):** score each KR 0.0–1.0, mark met/partial/missed, then keep · retire · add, and author the Q2 set.

## How the OKRs drive the week & month (summer)
This is the point of the whole system — the OKRs set the priorities, not the inbox.
- **The filter:** every block of weekly work should ladder to a KR or a pillar. If a chunk doesn't map to any pillar, question whether it's the unit's work.
- **In practice:** each person's weekly plan **leads with their KR next-actions** as the anchor priorities; reactive and service requests fill in *around* them, not over them.
- **The summer arc (the red → green march to the gate):**
  - **June** — stand up the engines: newsletter issue #1, dashboard unification, the decision-log habit, repo schema. (Today's 🔴 KRs.)
  - **July** — build & deliver: repo MVP (Jul 31), partner formalized, white-paper draft started, practice-load framework finalized for camp.
  - **August** — adopt & run: dashboard in real weekly use (FB + VB), framework live for fall camp, decision log filling → **gate**.

## Tracking — the scoreboard tool
Status lives in **`okr-tracker/`** (see its README), not in hand-maintained tables. Each Thursday, log what moved:
```bash
python okr-tracker/okr.py check <KR> <confidence 0.0–1.0> <green|yellow|red|met> "<note>" --next "<next action>" [--blocker "..."]
```
That regenerates **`okr-tracker/SCOREBOARD.md`** — status, confidence, progress bar, per-KR trend, and the current next action, grouped by objective. Confidence = P(hit target by gate).

## At the gate (end of August)
Set each KR's `score` (0.0–1.0 attainment) in `okrs.yaml`, mark met / partial / missed, then keep · retire · add and author the Q2 set.

# Insight Is Not a Control

> Writing down the correct diagnosis does nothing to prevent the thing you diagnosed. A recorded insight has no enforcement power — it decays at the same rate as no insight at all unless something outside your memory acts on it.

## Why it matters

The tempting response to a failure is to understand it, and understanding feels like progress. It isn't a control. A control is something that fires whether or not you remember it exists: a scheduled task, a gate, a check that runs on its own clock. Notes, frameworks, and resolutions are all in the "remember to apply" category, which means their reliability is capped by attention — the exact resource that was scarce when the failure happened.

This is the layer under [[standards-without-enforcement]]. That note says a rule without a forcing function is a suggestion. This one narrows it to the self: a rule you wrote *for yourself*, and agree with, is still a suggestion.

## Evidence / origin

On 2026-06-04 I wrote [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]]: *"A brief that is generated but not delivered fails exactly like no brief at all. If the output lands somewhere you have to remember to go look, the tool recreates the very cracks it was built to close."*

The daily interview and weekly review rituals stopped on **2026-06-05 — the next day** — and nothing surfaced that fact for **49 days**. The note was correct, recent, and specifically about this failure mode, and it did not protect the practice that produced it. It couldn't: the note had no surfacing mechanism either.

What actually held, once built, was a scheduled task that reads each ritual's own output as the record of when it last ran and raises a desktop prompt when overdue. It does not care whether I remember.

The asymmetry that makes the point: over the same 49 days, every cron-driven surface in three separate systems stayed current, and every manually-driven one froze. See [[automated-survives-manual-freezes]].

## Connections
- [[delivery-is-part-of-the-mechanism]] — this note updates it: surfacing must be *automatic*, not merely present
- [[standards-without-enforcement]] — same claim applied to organizations; this is the self-directed case
- [[the-daily-on-ramp]] — the on-ramp is only as reliable as the thing that triggers it
- [[automated-survives-manual-freezes]] — the empirical pattern this claim rests on

## Open questions

- Which of my other written resolutions are currently uncontrolled? A note that names a discipline but has no scheduled trigger is a candidate for the same 49-day silence.
- Is there a cheap way to make a note itself surface — a review cadence over `Notes/` — or does that just move the problem up a level?
- Does this generalize to athlete-facing work? A protocol staff agree with, documented and unenforced, may fail the same way the recovery-session attendance did.

=== README
# OKR Tracker

A dependency-light tracker for the [Applied Performance unit OKRs](../Applied-Performance-OKRs-2026-27.md). You edit data; the script renders a scoreboard. Everything is markdown/YAML, lives in the vault, and is backed up by `../../backup.sh`.

## Files
- **`okrs.yaml`** — the data you maintain (9 KRs, each with owner, target, and a list of weekly check-ins). **Hand-edit this.**
- **`okr.py`** — reads `okrs.yaml`, writes `SCOREBOARD.md`.
- **`SCOREBOARD.md`** — generated. **Don't hand-edit** (it gets overwritten).

## Weekly flow (Thursday check-in)
For each KR that moved, log a check-in two ways — pick whichever you prefer:

**A. Command (fast):**
```bash
python okr.py check 1.1 0.4 yellow "wired dashboard to GPS feed" --next "demo to VB staff" --blocker "VB buy-in"
```
`check <KR> <confidence 0.0-1.0> <green|yellow|red|met> "<note>" [--next "next action"] [--blocker "..."] [--date YYYY-MM-DD]`
It appends a dated check-in and regenerates the scoreboard.

**B. Edit `okrs.yaml` by hand**, then run:
```bash
python okr.py
```

> On Windows, if emoji/bars look garbled in the terminal, set `PYTHONUTF8=1` (the file is always written as UTF-8 regardless).

## Concepts
- **Confidence (0.0-1.0)** = your honest probability of hitting the target *by the gate*. Drives the progress bar and trend sparkline.
- **Status** = `green` on track · `yellow` at risk · `red` off track · `met` done.
- **Next action** = the single next step for the KR's co-owner before the next check-in. Rule: every KR always carries exactly one. Shown on the scoreboard.
- **Trend** = confidence across successive check-ins (▁→█), so you see momentum, not just the latest number.
- **score** (per KR, starts `null`) = the final 0.0-1.0 attainment you set at the **end-of-August gate**.

## At the gate (2026-08-31)
Set each KR's `score`, mark met/partial/missed, then keep · retire · add and author the Q2 set. See [[Applied-Performance-Operating-Cadence]].

# Automated Survives, Manual Freezes — and the System Still Looks Healthy

> In any system with both scheduled and manual processes, the scheduled ones stay current and the manual ones silently stop. The dangerous part is not the stopping — it's that the automated half keeps reporting green, so the system reads as healthy right up until someone asks the manual half a question.

## Why it matters

This makes "should I automate this?" a much sharper question. It isn't about saving effort; it's about survival odds. Anything you intend to do *repeatedly* and haven't given a trigger to, you will eventually stop doing — and you won't notice, because nothing errors when a ritual is skipped. A skipped process produces an **absence**, and absences are invisible. A failed process produces an **error**, and errors get fixed.

The corollary for auditing your own systems: don't ask "is everything running?" Ask "what here has no trigger?" That list is your decay set, and it's knowable in advance.

## Evidence / origin

Three independent systems audited on 2026-07-24, same pattern in each:

| System | Automated (cron-driven) | Manual |
|---|---|---|
| KeystoneOS | inventory, morning report, dashboard, backup — all current, all tasks returning 0 | hand-written routers frozen 45 days; one asserted a GitHub token was invalid that had been working for weeks |
| `~/.claude` | daily logs, transcripts, memory capture — all current | skill set regrew unwatched to ~10,700 tokens loaded every session |
| SecondBrain | meeting sync (307 files), library ingest — current through that day | `Notes/` frozen 49 days; `Drafts/` and `Archive/` never used at all |

Every one of those systems would have passed a casual "is it working?" check, because the automated surfaces were genuinely healthy and they're the ones you look at.

=== README
# OKR Tracker

A dependency-light tracker for the [Applied Performance unit OKRs](../Applied-Performance-OKRs-2026-27.md). You edit data; the script renders a scoreboard. Everything is markdown/YAML, lives in the vault, and is backed up by `../../backup.sh`.

## Files
- **`okrs.yaml`** — the data you maintain (9 KRs, each with owner, target, and a list of weekly check-ins). **Hand-edit this.**
- **`okr.py`** — reads `okrs.yaml`, writes `SCOREBOARD.md`.
- **`SCOREBOARD.md`** — generated. **Don't hand-edit** (it gets overwritten).

## Weekly flow (Thursday check-in)
For each KR that moved, log a check-in two ways — pick whichever you prefer:

**A. Command (fast):**
```bash
python okr.py check 1.1 0.4 yellow "wired dashboard to GPS feed" --next "demo to VB staff" --blocker "VB buy-in"
```
`check <KR> <confidence 0.0-1.0> <green|yellow|red|met> "<note>" [--next "next action"] [--blocker "..."] [--date YYYY-MM-DD]`
It appends a dated check-in and regenerates the scoreboard.

**B. Edit `okrs.yaml` by hand**, then run:
```bash
python okr.py
```

> On Windows, if emoji/bars look garbled in the terminal, set `PYTHONUTF8=1` (the file is always written as UTF-8 regardless).

## Concepts
- **Confidence (0.0-1.0)** = your honest probability of hitting the target *by the gate*. Drives the progress bar and trend sparkline.
- **Status** = `green` on track · `yellow` at risk · `red` off track · `met` done.
- **Next action** = the single next step for the KR's co-owner before the next check-in. Rule: every KR always carries exactly one. Shown on the scoreboard.
- **Trend** = confidence across successive check-ins (▁→█), so you see momentum, not just the latest number.
- **score** (per KR, starts `null`) = the final 0.0-1.0 attainment you set at the **end-of-August gate**.

## At the gate (2026-08-31)
Set each KR's `score`, mark met/partial/missed, then keep · retire · add and author the Q2 set. See [[Applied-Performance-Operating-Cadence]].

# Automated Survives, Manual Freezes — and the System Still Looks Healthy

> In any system with both scheduled and manual processes, the scheduled ones stay current and the manual ones silently stop. The dangerous part is not the stopping — it's that the automated half keeps reporting green, so the system reads as healthy right up until someone asks the manual half a question.

## Why it matters

This makes "should I automate this?" a much sharper question. It isn't about saving effort; it's about survival odds. Anything you intend to do *repeatedly* and haven't given a trigger to, you will eventually stop doing — and you won't notice, because nothing errors when a ritual is skipped. A skipped process produces an **absence**, and absences are invisible. A failed process produces an **error**, and errors get fixed.

The corollary for auditing your own systems: don't ask "is everything running?" Ask "what here has no trigger?" That list is your decay set, and it's knowable in advance.

## Evidence / origin

Three independent systems audited on 2026-07-24, same pattern in each:

| System | Automated (cron-driven) | Manual |
|---|---|---|
| KeystoneOS | inventory, morning report, dashboard, backup — all current, all tasks returning 0 | hand-written routers frozen 45 days; one asserted a GitHub token was invalid that had been working for weeks |
| `~/.claude` | daily logs, transcripts, memory capture — all current | skill set regrew unwatched to ~10,700 tokens loaded every session |
| SecondBrain | meeting sync (307 files), library ingest — current through that day | `Notes/` frozen 49 days; `Drafts/` and `Archive/` never used at all |

Every one of those systems would have passed a casual "is it working?" check, because the automated surfaces were genuinely healthy and they're the ones you look at.

**Plan type:** architectural. That means it is a process plus an automatic check, not a one-file change. Tell me if you want it smaller.

**What I found.** You already built the OKR system you described today. It died in pieces:

- **6/12:** the OKR tracker stopped. The Thursday check-in needed Blake, and Blake left.
- **8/14:** the morning brief was retired. It was written every day, but nothing put it in front of you.
- **8/31:** the summer goals were due to be scored. They are still not scored, 14 days later.
- **9/7:** status report #2 was written. It was never sent.
- **5/22 and 7/31:** those notes gave good rules, but nothing triggered them.

Each one needed you to remember it. Your timed jobs still run: the GPS pull, the CFB capture, and the backup. Your notes `insight-is-not-a-control` and `automated-survives-manual-freezes` say the same thing.

There is also a second gap. No part of the old system ever said "not yet" to a new project. You have 18 active projects right now.

**My question: why did the old fixes stop?**

1. **"I had to remember them."** Then I build a timer, not another doc. I would add a check to your existing nag job, `KeystoneOS/scripts/ritual-check.ps1`. It would warn you when the OKR score is overdue. It would also warn you when you have more active projects than your limit (for example, 1 per pillar). Then we do the overdue 8/31 scoring together, and we use it to write the fall goals.
2. **"Something else."** Tell me what it was. For example: the goals were wrong, the work kept changing, or Chris and Kenny never pulled on it.

I pick **option 1**, because your files show that pattern five times. But only you can say if it is the real reason. The other open question is also yours to answer: why is now different?
